items.title: Why Jordan Cox refuses to take a breather: ‘If England want me, I’ll be there’

Cox, recently handed a two-year central contract after a breakout summer, was having none of it.

items.title: Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling
items.summary:
Midfielder’s under-21s winner eclipsed Jude Bellingham’s mark and there was other talent to admire against France

There may have been an Mbappé on the pitch – Ethan, the younger brother of Kylian, with whom he shares a near-identical gait – but by the end there was only one precocious talent on the lips of those watching England overcome France in their under-21s clash. Max Dowman had done it again, lighting up another game, this time in filthy conditions at Ashton Gate. It was fitting he had the final say in a 3-2 win. The noise that accompanied his match-winning goal? Well, beyond the palpable excitement in the stands in Bristol, that would be the sound of the teenager sending yet another record tumbling.

Which one takes your fancy? Take your pick. At 14, playing for Arsenal’s under-19s, he became the Uefa Youth League’s youngest goalscorer. This time last year, after taking to the field at Slavia Prague aged 15 and 308 days, Dowman became the youngest player to feature in the Champions League. In March, six months on from his professional debut, he became the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer. He is the youngest player to earn a Premier League winner’s medal. Last month he was presented with three Guinness World Records.

Continue reading...
items.t: Max Dowman shines in England colours and sends another record tumbling

items.title: The Breakdown | Rattled All Blacks face rare twin threat as England eye back-to-back scalps
items.summary:
After their seismic defeat by Wales, New Zealand face the prospect of history repeating itself in unwanted ways

They still talk about the last – and only – time the All Blacks have contrived to lose twice in succession to England. Back in 2002-03, as now, there was a Rugby World Cup looming in Australia and New Zealand had no shortage of quality players. “There is so much talent in New Zealand that, if they don’t win the World Cup, there should be an inquiry,” opined Steve Hansen, Wales’s head coach at the time, ahead of England’s fateful visit to Wellington in the summer of 2003.

There’s a fresh inquiry under way now even before the All Blacks trot out of the Twickenham tunnel this weekend for the 48th meeting between the two nations. While Saturday’s 35-28 defeat to Wales ended a 73-year wait from a home perspective it has inevitably precipitated plenty of dark muttering back in the land of the long flat white.

Continue reading...
items.t: The Breakdown | Rattled All Blacks face rare twin threat as England eye back-to-back scalps

items.title: ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award
items.summary:
By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience

Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria in 2022. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”

Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to BigShoe’s initiative.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award

items.title: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta
items.summary:
Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead

Thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It said he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

items.t: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

items.title: I built a reputation as a ‘walker’ so I could cheat when it mattered most – and it worked | The Secret Cricket Coach
items.summary:
Cricket always celebrates sportsmanship and condemns cheating, but where exactly is the line between the two?

I once played in a one-day semi-final. We were in a very tight spot when I edged the ball to the keeper. I didn’t walk. The opposition couldn’t believe it. They crowded around me, furious, and I was getting plenty of abuse.

I managed to get a single and when I reached the other end the umpire said: “You didn’t nick that did you? You are a walker.” “Yep, that’s right,” I replied.

items.title: Fifa accused of climate ‘record of failure’ due to Aramco deal and tournament expansion
items.summary:
• Groups question ‘sincerity’ to meet emissions pledges

  • Oil giant is a major sponsor of football governing body

The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action.

Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”.

As he prepares to depart for Manchester United, the outgoing US coach held court on a number of topics, including what he’d change about soccer in America

Outgoing US head coach Mauricio Pochettino and former Manchester City head coach Pep Guardiola have a long, storied past. The two faced each other as players, when Guardiola was at Barcelona and Pochettino was making his name across town at Espanyol. They faced each other 22 times as managers in the Premier League and the two share a mutual respect – and intensity – when it comes to their approach to playing and coaching alike.

So when Guardiola visited Yankee Stadium in September to serve as New York City FC’s pre-match hype man before their rivalry match with Red Bull New York, Pochettino – in town anyways to scout the match – made it a point to sit with him during the game. He brought along his assistant coach and confidant Jesús Pérez, and US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson.

items.title: Rugby League World Cup was a triumph in Australia and invisible in the UK | Aaron Bower
items.summary:
No free-to-air coverage and uncompetitive teams meant England fans all but missed a tournament that caught fire in the southern hemisphere

So, that was the Rugby League World Cup. It may have gripped you from start to finish or it may have passed you by without recognising it was even happening. It probably depends on where you are in the world: the tournament showcased many things but perhaps most of all the widening gulf between the two hemispheres.

There have been some magnificent positives. The primary one appears to be that those in charge in Australia – soon to be in charge in England, but more on that shortly – have realised there is value in international rugby league. For too long the National Rugby League has disregarded the international game, but it has come alive again in recent years.

items.t: Rugby League World Cup was a triumph in Australia and invisible in the UK | Aaron Bower

Sport has been more visible at the latest climate crisis summit in Antalya than most others. The stakes couldn’t be higher

If Cop is the Olympics of climate diplomacy, Antalya has made getting to the starting line an event in itself. Transport has been such an endurance test at the UN climate summit that anyone who reaches the venue in Turkey deserves a medal.

Inside, the athletic achievements are less obvious. There are no world records for removing square brackets from negotiating texts, though anyone watching bleary-eyed delegations attempt it may think there should be.

items.t: Cop31 summit spells out stark warnings for athletes and sport organisations

items.title: Brock Purdy was once dismissed as a system guy. Now he is THE guy
items.summary:
The San Francisco 49ers quarterback was long seen as the beneficiary of the tools at his disposal. This season, he’s setting fire to that narrative

The Dallas Cowboys entered this week having given up the second-most points in the NFC, but there was a particular elegance to the beating Brock Purdy put on them as the San Francisco 49ers moved to 8-1 with a 46-40 shootout win in front of a sullen Jerry Jones in north Texas. Purdy has presided over lots of routs since he took over the offense in 2022, but this particular defeat of the Cowboys had a unique feel to it.

Purdy, who is often dismissed as benefiting from a hospitable 49ers system, was a wrecking crew. That was true in the statistical sense, as Purdy closed with 389 yards and three touchdowns on 22-of-28 passing. Later in the game, it became true in the literal sense as Purdy ended one of his greatest games in style.

Continue reading...
items.t: Brock Purdy was once dismissed as a system guy. Now he is THE guy

items.title: Wales’ epic upset against All Blacks offers fresh hope for rank outsiders | Robert Kitson
items.summary:
The plot twist in Cardiff that nobody saw coming suggests the northern hemisphere is remobilising in time for next year’s World Cup

What does it take to beat the All Blacks in Cardiff? “I’ll never forget the pressure they put us under. I don’t think we were a better team than New Zealand, but there was a certain spirit in the Welsh side which pulled us through.” The vivid recollections of the late, great Cliff Morgan on Wales’s famous victory in 1953 could just as easily have applied to the long-awaited modern-day sequel on Saturday.

Seventy-three years. The last time it came to pass was the year Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay officially became the first people to conquer Everest. Some bookmakers had even stopped taking bets on an All Blacks win; in the buildup the Wales side were likened in one New Zealand newspaper to “Dickensian orphans” begging for scraps. More bread of heaven, please sir? Here was a plot twist nobody saw coming.

items.t: Wales’ epic upset against All Blacks offers fresh hope for rank outsiders | Robert Kitson

items.title: European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks
items.summary:
Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome

It will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino.

Continue reading...
items.t: European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks
